env.note: Measured on the corpus's Apple M5 Pro (arm64) — the canonical host. The earlier x86-64 Linux cloud-container run is preserved verbatim in results.container-x86.json for anyone re-running a regression on that host; its absolute times/sizes/RSS are NOT comparable here (different ISA + toolchains). RESOLUTION of the container's flagged RC gap: the container measured kara RC ~1.09x behind Rust Rc and flagged it for the M5 re-bench before treating as a tracked regression — on the M5 that gap VANISHES. kara RC 237.8ms vs equal-semantics Rust Rc 235.7ms is a statistical tie (1.009x, overlapping sigma); kara's entire +7% over Rust Box (222.2ms) is the RC-vs-unique-ownership cost that Rust itself pays going Box->Rc (+6%), not kara codegen overhead. Machine flip worth noting: Go went from slowest on the container (527ms, GC) to FASTEST on M5 (163.2ms) — its bump allocator + GC wins on fast cores for this build-heavy tree workload. No tracked regression.

kata.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
kata.workload: build 4 balanced 2047-node trees once, then 40000 full root-to-leaf DFS traversals. Depth is bounded on purpose: each path spells a base-10 number so a depth-18 tree overflows i64 outright and kara traps overflow, aborting rather than measuring; at depth 11 the leaf sum stays near 1e14. The punch count carries the workload instead. NOTE: this is the corpus's only shared-struct (RC) tree kata -- kara and the Rust mirror (Rc) both pay retain/release traffic during the traversal, while Go (GC pointers) and C (raw malloc'd pointers) do not. kara's RC-elision optimization is worth 34.6% here, measured by rebuilding with KARAC_RC_ELIDE_REF_PARAMS=0.

kata.title: Surrounded Regions
kata.workload: build one 300x300 grid at ~50% 'O' density once, then 400 punches; each punch copies the pristine grid into a working grid and runs the full solve (border flood-fill with an explicit position stack, then the relabel sweep) and hashes the result. The copy is deliberately inside the measured region: solve mutates the board, and the alternatives are a per-iteration refill loop or extra un-mutation work; a straight copy is the same O(rows*cols) order as the solve and every lane pays it identically. Density is load-bearing -- much sparser and the floods terminate immediately, much denser and the whole grid becomes one border-connected component. NOTE: all four lanes use a genuinely nested board (array of row pointers / Vec<Vec> / [][]), not a flat block, so C gets no locality advantage.

kata.title: Palindrome Partitioning
kata.workload: four 16-character case strings built once, then 150 punches of the full backtracking enumeration. String shape IS the workload: an all-'a' string of length n has 2^(n-1) palindromic partitionings, so the search is exponential in n and two characters change the runtime fourfold. The set mixes all-'a' (maximum branching, every substring is a palindrome), alternating abab (moderate), a no-repeat string (minimum, only single characters) and a structured aabaac pattern, so no single extreme of the search tree dominates. NOTE: the kata's substring is O(n) -- it walks the characters and filters rather than slicing -- and every mirror reproduces that per-piece cost rather than using a native O(1) slice, which would make C/Rust/Go a different algorithm.

kata.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
kata.workload: four 500-character case strings built once over alphabets of size 2, 4, 26 and 3, then 400 punches of the full O(n^2) DP. Alphabet size is the knob: a 2-letter alphabet makes the palindrome table dense so the cut loop scans many true entries, while 26 letters make almost nothing a palindrome and the inner loop exits early -- the set spans both so neither branch of the pal[0][i] test dominates. This is the DP sibling of #131: that kata enumerates every partitioning and is dominated by per-piece String allocation, while this one only needs the minimum cut count, so a table replaces the backtracking and the cost becomes a flat O(n^2) fill with no allocation in the inner loops. Benching both separates kara on String churn from kara on a dense 2-D table. NOTE: all lanes use a genuinely nested bool table (row pointers / Vec<Vec<bool>> / [][]bool), not a flat block or a packed bitset.

kata.title: Gas Station
kata.workload: build 8 gas/cost array pairs of 200000 elements once, then 1200 punches of the greedy single pass. Half the pairs are feasible (costs drawn from a smaller range than gas) and half are not; both walk the entire array since the algorithm has no early exit, but they differ in how often the tank<0 restart fires, which is the only branch in the loop. NOTE: the bench passes the arrays by reference where the kata takes Vec[i64] by value -- by value would copy 200000 elements per call, which no mirror does and which would swamp the O(n) scan being measured.

kata.title: Candy
kata.workload: build 8 ratings arrays of 200000 elements once, alternating narrow (4-value) and wide (100000-value) ranges, then 150 punches of both greedy passes plus the sum. Rating spread is the knob: a narrow range gives long runs of equal ratings where neither greedy rule fires and both passes are pure scans, while a wide range gives frequent strict inequalities so the right-to-left pass does real max-taking work. This kata is the corpus's cleanest exercise of a DESCENDING loop -- the right-to-left pass walks i=n-2 down to 0 with an index-dependent condition -- a distinct bounds-check-elimination surface from the ascending loops elsewhere; every mirror uses an explicit descending index loop rather than a reverse iterator so the loop shape matches. NOTE: the bench passes ratings by reference where the kata takes Vec[i64] by value.
